column2: A powerful full moon floodlights the valley; such energy that no one can sleep; a walk along the dusty road, cast shadows, farm dogs on the alert; at the waterfall, let's go skinny-dipping!; joyful splashing, icy water, the brave under the falls, ghostly white bodies; teeth chattering, they dry off by capering about, dress in a hurry, walk for miles warming up, and come back at dawn. Words: “Let's go skinnnydipping!” Atmosphere: Silver moon, icy, exhilarating water, laughter, total freedom. Stakes: Inhibitions abandoned in a paradisal setting.

A quiet walk; only Hayes has seen the rattlesnake coiled behind a tall clump of grass; without a word he picks up a stone and kills it with a throw of deadly accuracy; the cook skins the snake and cooks it for Bodky's supper. Words: “Tastes like chicken”. Atmosphere: Calm broken by the singer's sure, swift gesture. Stakes: The trained eye of the legendary Black artist, protector of his friends.

Every evening, listening to the news surrounded by Europeans whose relatives are in danger; at table, three-quarters of the company slip without realizing it into French or German. Atmosphere: European charm, the anguish of war muted in the background. Stakes: The college as an island of wartime Europe in the American Arcadia.

On arriving, Weitzer neglects to reserve any furniture; all that is left is a creaking rail-back chair. He asks around: no one sympathizes. He is sent to the woodshop. There he finds independent spirits who pass on their ethic to him; he designs his sandwich table and hangs it from the ceiling, for lack of legs. Words: why not go up to the shop and make something?; the ethic of the shop: invent, be creative, don't copy, don't bother me Atmosphere: a total absence of sympathy, but a positive atmosphere; the solitary pride of an object unique in the world; a warm surge of creativity despite the screws that catch on legs and the hammock-like swaying Stakes: a novice's initiation into creative self-sufficiency

Hostile students slip a construction made of cow dung among the anonymous works; Albers goes down the row, praises some marbles that look like fish eggs, then reaches the dung: so real that one wants to pick it up and smell it to be sure — he smells it, and he is sure. Without blinking, he puts it down, skips his usual comment on color and form, and moves on. Words: Ah, a good fake: marbles that look like fish eggs... and this one? Wonderful — it looks like a real, muddy cow pat! So real that one wants to smell it to be sure... Atmosphere: tension, the students' silent provocation; Albers's imperturbable composure Stakes: who will give in: the master or the mutineers?

Wunsch, released from jail, waits until one in the morning and comes back for his belongings while the college sleeps; Molly, awake, listens to his little footsteps going back and forth with the books; she holds back the urge to go down and help him because she has been forbidden to; he leaves before dawn, for good, in his little roadster. Words: To Molly's protest: “Well, he wouldn't want to see anybody”. Atmosphere: night, muffled footsteps, sleeplessness, a moral closed room Stakes: The community takes part in the erasure of one of its own; a missed chance for solidarity

Molly, in charge after Dreier's departure, convenes the whole community despite the faculty's ban; Miller tells the truth about the arrest and presents the departure as a fait accompli; no one protests, neither students nor elders, although some are attached to him. Words: The unofficial version of a resignation for nervous exhaustion. Atmosphere: brutal truthfulness but general resignation Stakes: The truth told too late to save Wunsch

Straus, distrustful, meets Wallen in Baltimore and is pleasantly surprised; a second visit to the couple's home: a charming wife, restrained prints; he writes a flattering portrait and recommends the appointment. Words: Wallen “genuine,” does not talk like a printed book; a tenor's speaking voice, sings second bass; a soft, kind surface over a solid ground. Atmosphere: an entomologist's curiosity, then real sympathy Stakes: The college's future judged on a tone of voice

Tempted to replace Carl Rogers at the USO — a career and income boosted, but life in New York, little time for writing or family — Wallen declines and accepts Black Mountain, seeing in it a greater learning experience for himself and his wife. Words: Wallen wants to find out whether a better understanding of the dynamics of human behavior has any bearing on the effectiveness of democratic processes Atmosphere: An inner weighing of ambition against ideals Stakes: The arrival of the man who will submit the community to psychological examination

One summer evening, the tenor with the worn voice sings Monteverdi, Haydn, Mozart, Schubert, then spirituals and Creole and Afro-Brazilian songs, before a Black and white audience overflowing onto the porch Words: the audience will call the concert “beautiful beyond words” and one of the greatest moments in Black Mountain's history Atmosphere: a mild evening, a packed hall, the silent boldness of a racially mixed audience in the segregated South Stakes: the absence of the expected riot decides the fate of the college's integration experiment

The young neuropsychiatric technician works day after day among the mentally ill. Words: he learned how small the difference is between sanity and insanity, and that a combination of the two is essential. Atmosphere: Material for a flashback: the wards, the closeness of madness, before BMC. Stakes: Grounds the artist's relationship to the irrational, echoing Breton as a medical orderly at Saint-Dizier (1916).

After a month of work, Elaine slips her first art article — ten pages on Stuart Davis — into Denby's mailbox. The next day a one-word telegram arrives. Words: Telegram: “Magnificent”. Atmosphere: The excitement of a first critical work, the silence of the next day, then the burst of a single word. Stakes: The birth of a critic's vocation; she puts the article away, mission accomplished.

After six months of planning the new college, Foreman, very upset and ashamed, announces that he is becoming secretary of the National Citizens Political Action Committee Atmosphere: a painful confession, a hard blow for the penniless Cohens Stakes: the collapse of the rebels' dream

A former student turned architecture instructor, Beidler is appointed in February 1945 instructor and consulting architect; he designs the Music Cubicle, built the following summer. Consequences: Beidler leaves after the summer of 1945 to found his own firm; the plan for cubicles scattered across the campus abandoned
Installation view of Jane Slater's graduation exhibition in March 1945, photographed for the college's records.

Dreier suggests, without proof and without this view being considered at the time, that the sailor was an agent provocateur: Wunsch's reputation as a “Negrophile” infuriated the local police and judiciary, who had known of his homosexuality since an incident at the University of North Carolina; they supposedly set him up. Consequences: It remains a shared suspicion, without proof.

Wunsch had always done everything to hide his homosexuality: never any advances, never any confidences; he was thought to be psychologically a bit neuter, with no sexual appetite. The staff say they are shocked; three or four members profess indignation (how could he do this to us?), a sign that the institution's reputation is beginning to take precedence over the well-being of individuals.

Wunsch resigns at once, with no one trying to keep him. The college, warned by its lawyer not to make any official payment, buys his library so as to pass him 700 dollars — a solution at first disputed (Dreier to Stephen Forbes: paying more would look like an official absolution). In keeping with the agreement with the Board of Fellows, Wunsch comes back for his belongings only at one in the morning and leaves before the community wakes. Molly Gregory, awake, hears those little feet going back and forth, back and forth, carrying books, and regrets not going down to help him — she had been told she must not. With Dreier away on vacation at Lake George, Molly, the senior officer, defies the ban on telling the students the truth: Herbert Miller informs the community, the departure presented as a fait accompli. The official version cites overwork without vacations. 700 dollars, a library bought, 1 a.m., Lake George

Exposed as a homosexual, Wunsch is forced to leave the college secretly and ignominiously, an illustration of the prevailing code of silence. Consequences: An example in Duberman (pp. 225-27) of how this code worked

Released from jail, Wunsch keeps to the agreement: he waits until one in the morning to come for his belongings and leaves before the community wakes. Molly, awake in her room, hears his little footsteps going back and forth, back and forth, carrying books; she has been forbidden to intervene; she resists the impulse to go down and help him and will regret it all her life. Words: She had been told he would not want to see anybody; she had been told she must not. Atmosphere: Night, muffled footsteps, shame and reticence, the helpless compassion of a woman pinned to her bed. Stakes: Collective cowardice disguised as consideration; an individual conscience that cannot forgive itself for keeping silent.

Carol Brice, at the start of her career, who has come with her mother and her baby, stays four weeks; on the day of her last concert Roland Hayes arrives with his wife and daughter. Never having heard Brice, he is so taken with her that at a party at the Lowinskys' he sings her his own unpublished arrangements of Negro spirituals and promises to send her copies. Hayes, a magical storyteller and a charming man, stays two weeks and talks for hours about his experience as a Black man and about Black music. Fees and scholarships covered by the Julius Rosenwald Fund. a stay of 4 weeks (Brice) and 2 weeks (Hayes); funding from the Julius Rosenwald Fund Consequences: an enormous impact on the community

The largest crowd ever seen at the college — 400 people, 30 to 40 of them Black — arrives for Hayes; Lowinsky has briefed the ushers: extreme courtesy, and to the question of seating, the answer wherever you like. Integrated seating, no incidents; at the reception, a white woman murmurs that times have changed. Lowinsky has silenced the fear of the Klan. Words: Where should we sit? — Wherever you like.; “Times have changed, haven't they?” Atmosphere: tension under control, then silent triumph Stakes: integration put to the test before North Carolina; the gamble of risk

On the day of Brice's last concert, Hayes arrives with his wife and daughter; never having heard Brice, he is won over; at the party, he sings his own unpublished arrangements of Negro spirituals and promises copies for her concerts Atmosphere: a passing on between generations of Black singers, the intimacy of an evening Stakes: the handing on between the end and the beginning of a career
Mrs. Straus brings the news of the USSR's entry into the war against Japan, shortly after Martin's arrival.
Morning: Jalo and Bodky play Schoenberg (Op. 7) on two pianos. Afternoon: The Art of Fugue on strings. Evening: a slide show by Albers. It is raining. Three events on the same day; rain
In a taxi from Pennsylvania Station, Nina whistles out the window to greet Mike (Michael Kuttner), second violin of the Gordon String Quartet. A taxi, whistling through the window
Nina has an almost sensational success in the Fourth Brandenburg Concerto; the next day she goes on a picnic with her partners from the concert. A picnic in a pasture or on a summit

Before a landscape with a road, Mrs. Chareau speaks of the tenderness of telegraph poles; she notes the place's combination of poverty and luxury. John Reiss shows objective and nonobjective paintings that give Martin his first spontaneous pleasure before student work at BMC. A meal on the floor (hard-boiled eggs, salads, fruit, milk, cheese) for lack of chairs

At a meal, Kauder declares that movements born of a disintegrating world become absurd when transplanted to a healthy America, the most absurd thing being that the Europeans themselves come there to imitate; Martin, for his part, reflects that Dada, a farce of 1918, is now taught as the art of the masters. Words: Kauder's remark between an omelet and bread with honey. Atmosphere: Irony at table, friction between Europe and America. Stakes: What do the exiles really pass on?
Morning calm; Straus can be heard practicing the violin; three little clouds drift above three little hills. Atmosphere: Silence, the haze of violin sound, serenity.

Hayes, his voice declining, builds his recital through rhythm: the calculated pauses carry the listener through to the end. Words: Lowinsky: the movement is punctuated by the pause. Atmosphere: Rhythmic fascination.

In the fall of 1945, Elaine sets off on impulse with Bill Hardy, an engineering student who frequents the art world, to visit Edwin Denby, who spent his summers in Provincetown; the storm tosses the boat, and she wakes up on the leaking floor of the cabin; she insists the episode was platonic but apparently does not come back until early December, which infuriates Bill; according to Elaine, Hardy had never sailed and was “a pain in the neck”; Bill's biographers describe him as a seasoned sailor (disputed) Consequences: a marital crisis

Sylvesta Martin, from the Music Institute, becomes the first full-time Black woman student; Dr. Percy H. Baker of Virginia State College is hired as a visiting lecturer to teach biology in the fall term of 1945. The Julius Rosenwald Fund pays his salary of 700 dollars. In protest, R. R. Williams, the college's lawyer in Asheville and a member of the Advisory Council, resigns: he does not want to belong to an institution contrary to the enlightened public opinion of North Carolina. a salary of 700 dollars paid by the Rosenwald Fund

An impulsive departure by sailboat; the storm tosses the boat in the night; Elaine wakes up on the leaking floor of the cabin; she discovers that Hardy has never sailed Words: she will call him “a pain in the neck” Atmosphere: night, water coming in, seasickness Stakes: an escapade that wounds Bill and ends only in December

Despite the cracks in the marriage, the facade of happiness is kept up in the mail: the November letter to her father contains a lipstick kiss print from Elaine and photos of each of them a lipstick print, photos of both spouses

The studio Bill had lovingly renovated is taken from them after months of unpaid rent and the sale of the building; Bill and Conrad carry all their belongings by hand more than twenty blocks to the new apartment rolled-up linoleum balanced on the two men's shoulders; the new rent: 18 dollars a month, a five-floor walk-up Consequences: settling into a cold, unheated two-room flat on Carmine Street

A tiny unheated cold-water flat: a dangerous kerosene stove that must be cleaned often for fear that the soot will catch fire; they paint in opposite corners of a 10-by-15-foot room; Elaine notes that “cold-water” is a misnomer, since only the water was hot a kerosene stove; a 10x15-foot room; rent $18/month Consequences: minor irritations (Bill whistling classical themes) are magnified in this space
Between December 1945 and January 1946, Albers writes an unpublished article on art at Black Mountain College for Junior Bazaar magazine. Unpublished, JAAF archives.

To share the 35 dollars of monthly rent, Bill rents a studio on the third floor with Jack Tworkov; Elaine goes on painting alone in the Carmine Street flat, which also serves as the bedroom rent $35/month

At the end of 1946, Albers begins his first great color series, with a double title: Variants (borrowed from musical variations on a theme) and Adobes. Mexican colors — deep reds, golden yellows, vibrant pinks, burning oranges, the greens and browns of the earth, the saturated blues of the sky — invade his paintings. double titles: Variants / Adobes

At the end of 1946, Albers begins his first great color series, with a double title: Variants (borrowed from music, variations on a theme) and Adobes (a debt to vernacular architecture). Mexican colors: deep reds, golden yellows, bright pinks, warm oranges, set against greens, browns, and the saturated blues of the sky

Anni completes With Verticals, her last work on the scale of her earlier wall hangings, in threads of two main colors (deep red and rich gold) heightened by black passages, the “verticals”. Discontinuous weaving; a fusion of Peruvian textiles and the linear geometries of pre-Hispanic architecture

After a Saturday evening concert in which he had played (as pianist, it seems), Jalo goes for a drink at the Strauses', as he often does; on leaving he announces “going home now” and collapses on the lawn a few steps away, breathing his last there. Gretel finds this a beautiful death: filled with music, celebrating with good friends. the lawn, a few steps from the door Consequences: The Lowinskys' trip to Italy (Eddie's Guggenheim fellowship, 1946) is postponed by a year: the college asks Eddie to stay in the music department until August 1947.

A fellowship for Italy, postponed by a year because of Jalo's death (the college keeps Eddie until August 1947); Newhall teaches them to photograph manuscripts in preparation. Consequences: Departure for Italy in 1947.

Just after breakfast one weekday, at the end of the summer of 1946 (the Art Institute), a couple sets off with water and food toward the ridge. She called herself innocent before him; he was patient and attentive. On the way she points out wildflowers, birds, red lichen on the rocks. A patch of grass among the rock outcrops, an army blanket spread out, a deep blue sky, a view over the Swannanoa valley; they lower their voices and watch for strangers, to be safe. They make love, have lunch, sunbathe naked, and come back down without regret: an uncomplicated summer adventure. an army blanket, red lichen, spring water on the face, the Swannanoa valley

The night of Jalo's death strikes the community with despair. Woldin remembers his last concert and his transfigured face as he conducted “Jesu Meine Freude”; the students dig his grave and choose a stone with Johanna, and Ross Penley moves it with the tractor; Brahms's Requiem (“Behold all flesh is as the grass”) marks the mourning. a grave dug by hand, a stone chosen, a tractor, Brahms's Requiem

At the end of her first year, Molly Gregory announces her departure, leaving the shop without a keeper. Weitzer goes to see the powers that be and ends up with Rondy (Rondthaler), the business manager, who tells him to take charge of the shop himself. The agreement: Weitzer answers for the tools and materials, and the door stays unlocked. a negotiated condition: the shop door always open; Rondthaler worried that the tools will wander off and that the materials be accounted for Consequences: Weitzer becomes almost instantly the owner-manager of the woodworking shop; his career is launched; no thought given to insurance, accounting, or the school's image

Spring 1946: Jim Tite, a former professional jazz drummer turned early riser, notices at dawn that the woodworking shop building is a good dozen feet longer than the known interior space. A grimy window and a door locked with a cheap rusty padlock, made of three knotty boards, one of them loose; he forces his way in with a fallen branch. Inside: talcum-like dust, mildew, cobwebs, a cast-iron hand press with a treadle, an antique even in 1946 — a Challenge-Gordon — and a sloping rack with cases of jumbled type (“pi”: em quads, en quads, leads, and type mixed with the bodies of moths, flies, wasps, leaves, twigs, and acorns). He announces his discovery to “Rondy” (Rondthaler), who blesses the resurrection of the Black Mountain Press. A building 12 feet longer than expected; a 3-board door, a rusty padlock; a cast-iron Challenge-Gordon press; dead insects in the cases. Consequences: The rebirth of the college press.

Jim Tite shares his enthusiasm with Ann Mayer and evangelizes others. They spend their free hours cleaning the shop, enlarging it, sorting and redistributing the type, oiling the press, replacing the bearings of the bed, and installing a motor taken from a broken-down faculty Kelvinator. They make trips to Asheville to stand behind a local printer, ply him with questions, watch, and learn, before coming back to practice. A motor salvaged from a faulty faculty Kelvinator refrigerator. Consequences: The birth of a printing course.

Tite, knowing just enough to be dangerous, proposes to Rondthaler and Bill Levi a course in printing practice cotaught with Ann Mayer. He believes it was the college's first experience of teaching by students, a concept soon adopted by others (Harry Holl in sculpture, Arthur Penn in theater). One of his classes has twelve students, with the aim of covering all the college's printing needs so as to save it money. Harry Weitzer, from his first class, becomes an excellent coteacher. A class of 12 students. Consequences: Student teaching institutionalized.

They were planning to go to New York together at the end of the term; one morning, Kremen finds her hammering at an indistinct object. He asks her why she is working on the work program so early — the start of an anecdote about Black Mountain self-sufficiency (text cut off). A trip to New York planned for the end of the term.

After reading a report on BMC in the Partisan Review, Kremen rushes there. At sunrise, the train crosses the Smokies in the morning mist, and he glimpses a log cabin with smoke rising from its stone chimney: a landscape out of his childhood dreams, nourished by reading about early America. The feeling comes back at BMC during activities such as driving the cattle to pasture, felling trees, harvesting and husking corn, or fighting a forest fire on the mountain. a report in the Partisan Review; a log cabin, a stone chimney, smoke, morning mist

Noland's first year: logic and semantics with A. W. Levi, sociology with Herbert Miller, a tutorial in harmony with “Bimbus” Schlesinger, music theory with John Cage. Almost immediately he becomes a student of Bolotowsky (a Cubist approach), who teaches painting during Albers's sabbatical in Mexico. When Albers returns, he takes his design course (Bauhaus principles) — a decisive influence on his own teaching of design later at Catholic University in Washington. Consequences: an influence on his future teaching at Catholic University

Baker, described by a white colleague as courageous and likable, though very tense, is replaced in the second term by the Black composer Mark Fax. According to Lowinsky, both did splendid work, and their courses were well attended. No incident all year, a fact judged particularly remarkable given the stream of visitors and the repeated concerts by “Vesta” Martin and Fax before local people.

The students vote a resolution asking for the immediate admission of as many Black students as capacity allows, a broader recruitment campaign, the admission of Black men as well, and decide on a subscription during the Christmas vacation to help applicants without means. The faculty huffs a little but gives in to the argument: unanimous admission of Black men, and Lowinsky's contacts extended to Black high schools, newspaper editors, and local NAACP branches.

The students adopt a resolution asking for the immediate admission of as many Black students as capacity allows, a broader recruitment campaign, and the acceptance of Black men (until then only women). They also decide to run a fund-raising campaign during the Christmas vacation to offer financial aid to Black applicants unable to pay even minimal fees. A collection during the Christmas vacation Consequences: The faculty gives in to the argument and votes unanimously to add Black men to those eligible for admission

After the faculty vote, Lowinsky extends his contacts to Black high schools, newspaper editors, secretaries of local N.A.A.C.P. branches, the Y.M.C.A., and the interracial committee of the American Friends Service Committee. Consequences: Immediate but temporary results: five Black students enrolled for the 1947 winter session

Without any support from the faculty, according to an admiring student, Wallen urges the students to commit themselves concretely outside: one woman student spends two afternoons a week for a whole term with a young “schizophrenic” patient her own age in a nearby psychiatric hospital; others join the Southern Negro Youth Congress, carry petitions around the region, and try voter-registration work. Two afternoons a week; a two-mile walk to the bus stop each time; a whole term. Consequences: The college's contacts with the Black community and local racial issues increase.

Replaying the Bentley-Foreman scenario, several faculty members (above all the Europeans, Dehn and Albers among them) fear that Niebyl is using the racial question (the Southern Negro Youth Congress) as a cover to organize a communist cell; Niebyl despised the Communist Party's low scientific standards and apparently never joined. Niebyl arrives with three disciples. Consequences: The Board's decision not to renew his contract.

A telegram addressed to a woman student is opened by mistake by someone else; word goes round that it contains the number forty-seven — exactly the number of votes a proposal had received the day before at a community meeting. The conclusion is drawn that the Niebyl “plot” is under way and communicating with the outside. The student, subjected to a bizarre inquisition, reveals that the telegram came from a reactionary Republican friend and had nothing to do with the campus. The number 47; a telegram; a community meeting the day before. Consequences: An episode so absurd that it fuels the protest against Niebyl's dismissal.

When his one-year appointment expires, the Board decides unanimously not to extend Niebyl. A petition from 61 students out of 90 protests: no sufficient reason has been given, and his courses left ample room for the expression of opinions; they ask for the fullest consideration and a community meeting. The Board curtly rejects the petition: no new point, no further statement, and a community meeting would lead only to personal discussions. 61 signatures out of 90 students; a unanimous vote of the Board. Consequences: A rare case in which the Board goes against majority feeling and refuses discussion; Wallen and Levi convince the petitioners that politics did not motivate the decision.

After a zero-communication interview with Albers, who accuses him of wanting a “takeover,” Wallen reads a written statement opening with his wish to bring things into the open; in it he recalls that Albers called him “The Kaiser” earlier in the year, diagnoses that his fears outweigh his judgment rather than any deliberate malice, and mocks the man who, fearing conflict and dissension, acts in ways that encourage them. Albers's nickname for him: “The Kaiser”. Consequences: Only a momentary clarification.

At the end of the spring of 1946, the college adopts the proposals of the Wallen-Levi-Rondthaler committee: an eight-member Community Council (three teachers, three students, one representative of the wives and employees, one of the whole community — who may be a student) choosing the committees (publications, concerts, library), dealing with student housing, the cleanliness of the campus, and standards of community conduct, and calling community meetings on petition. A referendum can repeal any unpopular legislation by a two-thirds majority. The report also proposes a disciplinary committee with equal numbers of students and teachers and final power of expulsion, and a simple majority vote at faculty meetings when the traditional consensus fails. 8 members; two-thirds for a referendum; parity of students and teachers on the disciplinary committee. Consequences: A democratization seen by the fearful as a palace revolution; Wallen elected chairman of the Council the following month.
The month after his statement, Wallen is elected chairman of the new council, which seems to the suspicious to consolidate his power still further. Consequences: Strengthens Albers's distrust.

A student reports to Wallen that Albers discussed the Council elections with him, spoke of Wallen's “bid for power,” and visited some of his advisees to support his preferred student candidates. Wallen points out to the faculty that these are the very tactics Albers reproached the Bentleyites for two years earlier (interference in the election of the Student Moderator the previous year). Consequences: Open conflict between Albers and Wallen.

At the end of his first year, Wallen decides not to complete the requirements of his Harvard doctorate, believing that a heightened awareness of psychological concepts can lead some people to an unhealthy introspection: analyzing instead of living. Consequences: Shows Wallen's doubts about psychology, which Albers does not see.

Lacking the money to build (the interior of the Studies Building remains unfinished), Rondthaler obtains three buildings from the government: student studies, classrooms and storage, and the third, the most elegant, becomes the college's first properly lighted library — to the great joy of Nell Rice, its longtime librarian. 3 buildings; a lighted library; Nell Rice Consequences: increased capacity

The government donates a printing press, library and office furniture, two typewriters, a new dishwasher, a meat grinder — and, with its genius for the inappropriate, a hundred swivel chairs, a sewer cleaner, and a very large steam trouser press. a press, 2 typewriters, a dishwasher, a grinder, 100 swivel chairs, a sewer cleaner, a steam trouser press

Dreier, the dreamer in chief, imagines a fifteen-year program accommodating the 125-150 students he judges necessary for financial health. Unable to find a resident architect, the college hires The Architects Collaborative of Cambridge, a young group with which Gropius has associated himself, for the site plans and the general scheme. 15 years; 125-150 students targeted Consequences: the matrix of the campus's future development

Jalowetz dies in early 1946; Lowinsky accepts a Guggenheim fellowship and then leaves for Queens College. The department is saved in part by the hiring of Charlotte “Bimbus” Schlesinger (trained in Berlin, Vienna, and Russia, seven years at the Foxhollow School) and by Mrs. Jalowetz, who trains a few students in singing and gives a bookbinding course that some take out of affection for her. Consequences: The 1947 summer institutes almost suspended.

In 1946, Katherine Litz had danced in Cunningham's “The Princess Zonilda and Her Entourage,” a single concert at Hunter; their paths do not cross again until 1952 at BMC. A concert at Hunter College Consequences: A reunion in 1952 at BMC (material for an echo)

Wallen, an idealistic 28-year-old psychologist trained at Harvard, hired in 1945, wanted to impose more order on the college; Albers feared that his taste for efficiency and well-defined structures would stifle variety and spontaneity. Wallen: 28, Harvard Consequences: an increasingly conflict-ridden climate

Answering letters from Ted and Bobbie Dreier about the college's problems, Albers admits to growing doubts about his ability to do what is right for himself and for the college; he criticizes those who put governing before serving and aim to look important as much as to be so; he demolishes Wallen; he reaffirms that good teaching depends on personality and experience more than on method and equipment; he hates equalization for its own sake; after 13 years of putting the college before his own needs, approaching 60, he must think of his public obligations. Approaching 60; 13 years in the college's service; the phrase: “I hate equalization for equalizations sake”; an appeal to “common sense” and to “organizing oneself before organizing others” Consequences: Gives form to the unease that will lead to his 1949 resignation

The correspondence between the two old friends, cut off during the war, resumes; Albers sends care packages, clothes, and Mexican coffee; Perdekamp says he is more concerned about the wreck of German intellectual life than about comfort; he admires Albers for having freed himself so early from historicism. Perdekamp discovers Thomas Wolfe, who contrasts a weighed-down German culture with an America where time flows Consequences: The 1924 essay Historisch oder Jetzig made topical again
To make the angles studied clearly distinct, Albers has the students stand up and hold their pencils at 30, 45, and 60 degrees. Photograph of Albers and the students holding their pencils, 1946
A group photo of the faculty of the summer Art Institute, with Jean Varda perched in a tree. Varda photographed in a tree

A series of photographs: Albers examining a folded-paper construction with students, handling a sheet of paper with them, the students holding up their pencils to study angles. pencils held out to measure angles

Blumeneau, Lindenfeld, and Zeisler study with Albers in the summer of 1946; with Guermonprez, four women share the workshop, with rich conversations about preindustrial techniques Zeisler built up a collection of non-Western art, rich in pre-Columbian textiles Consequences: Their later influence: Blumeneau a textile curator at the Cooper-Hewitt, Lindenfeld tapestries and teaching in Japan

Despite divergent formal and philosophical approaches, Josef Albers invites Jacob Lawrence to teach at the 1946 Summer Art Institute; he comes with his wife, the painter Gwendolyn Knight Lawrence a photo of the couple by Beaumont Newhall in the summer of 1946 Consequences: the encounter leads Lawrence to intensify his work on line, form, color, and texture; he will call himself a direct descendant of the Bauhaus and credit Albers as one of the great masters of our time
Karnes studies with Josef Albers and Molly Gregory during the 1946 summer session; she will be the only American studio ceramist to have been both a student and a teacher at the college.
The catalogs published every year since 1934 stop after 1946; stapled brochures of identical format, staged photographs of college life, the seal designed by Albers.
Moholy-Nagy hires the young, relatively inexperienced photographer at the Institute of Design; the Callahans leave Detroit for Chicago.

Junius Bird, curator of archaeology at the American Museum of Natural History in New York, excavates a site containing textiles dating from 2500 B.C., including a piece with a bird formed by floating warp threads in a field of plain weave. textiles dated to 2500 B.C.; a piece depicting a bird; floating warp threads in a field of plain weave Consequences: Anni Albers makes it a major example of the direct formal language of threads

Young friends of Anni Albers tell her, in the year before 1947, about Gropius's opening address for the new term at Harvard: what struck them was the experience of perceiving sense and meaning in a confused world — the same experience of orientation as at the Bauhaus. Consequences: A parallel drawn by Anni between 1922 and 1946

Settles in Los Angeles, works briefly as an illustrator for a Westwood newspaper, then as a packing clerk at the Ballerina bathing-suit factory, where he meets Pat Pearman, an assistant designer, who, after seeing his drawings, convinces him that he has talent. The Ballerina Bathing Suit factory Consequences: The decision to become an artist

Photo of Lawrence and Gwendolyn Knight by Beaumont Newhall, summer 1946 Consequences: The lasting influence of Albers's teaching on Lawrence as a teacher

Summer Art Institute: alongside Anni and Josef Albers teach the painter Jacob Lawrence, Jean Varda, the sculptor Leo Amino, the architect Bertrand Goldberg (a former Bauhaus member, invited because Walter Gropius could come only to lecture), and the historian of photography Beaumont Newhall, just out of MoMA. Maya Deren is invited for a film series organized by Albers and Newhall but cannot come. More than sixty students enrolled, among them Ruth Asawa, Joseph Fiore, and Ray Johnson. Consequences: The April 1946 issue of Design magazine, devoted to the college, greatly increases interest and enrollment.
Walter Gropius can come in the summer of 1946 only for a lecture; Bertrand Goldberg, another former Bauhaus member, is invited to teach in his place.

After the year is over, Grice finds the family a small rough-wood cabin on the property of Boone Hall Plantation, an eighteenth-century estate whose main house was rebuilt in 1935. Rice sets up his writing desk in one of the nine one-room brick cabins, remnants of the plantation's slave quarters. Plenty of pecan and fig trees, a good vegetable garden, crab caught from a nearby dock; Rice's cooking skills Consequences: The harvests supplement the family's meager income.

Graham, a former Tsarist aristocrat, abandons psychoanalysis for esoteric and magical systems, vilifies abstraction, and venerates the old masters; in a four-page manifesto titled The case of Mr. Picasso (statements made in an interview of January 15, 1942), he accuses Picasso of being a “hoax” and an international money factory. A 4-page manifesto, circulated in 1946 Consequences: A break with his earlier modernist commitments
